title: Bartholomew (24 August)
hookLine: the apostle often identified with Nathanael, a man without guile

lines: CAN ANY THING OF GOOD COME FROM NAZARETH?
cards: "Can any thing of good come from Nazareth?" Those are Nathanael's first words about Jesus, before they've even met.
His friend Philip has just found him with big news: we have found the one Moses and the prophets wrote about, Jesus of Nazareth. Nathanael answers with a put-down of the man's hometown. It's rude.
It's also completely honest. And Philip doesn't argue. He just says three words: come and see.
Today, the apostle kept on the twenty-fourth of August, and the honest skeptic who may be the same man.

teach.h: BARTHOLOMEW IN THE LISTS, NATHANAEL IN JOHN.
teach.b: First, a puzzle. Matthew, Mark and Luke list a Bartholomew among the twelve apostles, named right beside Philip, but never tell a single story about him. John never uses the name Bartholomew at all.
Instead, John tells about Nathanael, brought to Jesus by Philip. So tradition puts the two together: one man. Nobody can prove it.
It's a reasoned guess, held openly, and the Church reads this very story on his feast. Now the story.
Before Nathanael can say anything, Jesus says of him, in the Douay-Rheims: "Behold an Israelite indeed, in whom there is no guile."
Guile is an old word for trickery: a hidden angle, saying one thing and meaning another. Jesus doesn't scold him for the crack about Nazareth. He names what was good in it: a man with nothing hidden.
Nathanael is startled: how do you know me?
Jesus says he saw him under the fig tree, before Philip ever called him. The Gospel never says what happened under that fig tree. Whatever it was, it lands.
Nathanael's doubt turns, on the spot, into faith: "Rabbi, thou art the Son of God."
Same honesty, new direction. Tradition adds that Bartholomew preached far from home and died a martyr, by some accounts flayed alive, which is why paintings sometimes show him holding a knife.
The Gospels don't tell any of that.

teach.h: AN ISRAELITE INDEED, IN WHOM THERE IS NO GUILE.
teach.b: What they keep is one moment: an honest doubter, a friend who said come and see, and a man without guile.

how: Catholics keep the feast of Saint Bartholomew, apostle, on 24 August; the Gospel read at Mass that day is the calling of Nathanael from the first chapter of John.

o: the brother of Peter who fished in Galilee

p: can any thing of good come from Nazareth?

s: the name Bartholomew appears in John's Gospel
John never uses it. he tells of Nathanael, and tradition joins the two.
Nathanael's first words about Jesus were a put-down of Nazareth
"can any thing of good come from Nazareth?" and Jesus still calls him a man without guile.
the Gospels tell how Bartholomew died
they don't. his preaching and martyrdom come from later tradition.

games.q: you're Philip. your friend sneers that nothing good comes from Nazareth. what do you say?
o: argue him down with the prophets.
drop it and go on alone.
games.why: Philip doesn't argue. he says "come and see," and the doubter goes with him, and ends up calling Jesus the Son of God.

practice: Bring to mind one place where you've been working an angle: a compliment you didn't mean, a reason that wasn't the real reason, a smile that covered something.

Don't punish yourself; just see it plainly, the way Jesus saw Nathanael under the fig tree, and ask what it would look like with nothing hidden. If you pray, bring it to God just as it is; if not, simply hold it in the light.

wordCard.voice: Bartholomew. The apostle named beside Philip, whom tradition identifies with Nathanael, the man Jesus called without guile.

orig.note: Greek: bait, a trick, deceit. in John 1:47, Nathanael is the man with none.

carryVoice: Your line: without guile. Philip didn't argue; he said come and see. See you tomorrow.
